title: GalaxEye Launches World's First OptoSAR Satellite Aboard SpaceX Falcon 9
excerpt: Bengaluru startup's Mission Drishti combines radar and optical sensors on a single platform, marking India's largest privately built satellite.
body:
• GalaxEye's 190-kg Drishti satellite, launched May 3 from Vandenberg on a Falcon 9, is the world's first to fuse synthetic aperture radar and optical sensors on one platform.
  • Founded by five IIT Madras graduates, the startup plans to scale to a 10-satellite constellation by 2030 for all-weather, sub-daily Earth observation.
  • The dual-use satellite targets defence, agriculture, disaster response, and maritime monitoring — sectors where the Indian diaspora's technical and investment ties are deepening.

Bengaluru-based GalaxEye Space launched its Mission Drishti satellite on May 3 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The 190-kg spacecraft — India's largest privately built satellite — rode as part of the CAS500-2 rideshare mission carrying 45 payloads into sun-synchronous orbit at roughly 500 km altitude.

What sets Drishti apart is its OptoSAR architecture: an X-band synthetic aperture radar delivering up to 0.9-metre resolution in spotlight mode, paired with a seven-band multispectral optical imager at 3.6-metre ground sampling distance. The onboard SyncFusion system fuses both data streams into a single, analysis-ready product in under 10 minutes — eliminating the need for separate radar and optical satellites, according to YourStory.

Context

GalaxEye was founded in 2021 by five IIT Madras graduates who first gained attention as finalists in the 2019 SpaceX Hyperloop competition. The company raised $3.5 million in seed funding in late 2022, followed by a $10 million Series A round led by MountTech Growth Fund in November 2024. Infosys also invested roughly $2 million in September 2024.

https://x.com/SpaceX/status/2083414597738897621

Before Drishti, the team validated its core technology through the GLX-SQ payload, launched aboard ISRO's POEM-4 platform on a PSLV-C60 rocket in December 2024. That demonstration tested the SyncFusion Imaging System under the harsh radiation conditions of the South Atlantic Anomaly and confirmed the payload could process and compress SAR data in orbit.

"GalaxEye has achieved what only a few global players have, which is seamlessly combining optical and SAR capabilities on a single platform to enable persistent, all-weather intelligence."

— Lt Gen AK Bhatt (Retd), Director General, Indian Space Association

The five years of indigenous R&D that led to Drishti's launch underscore the maturation of India's private space sector since the 2020 reforms that opened the industry to startups. India now operates 29 active Earth observation satellites under government programmes, and Drishti is expected to complement that fleet.

Impact

As a dual-use platform, Drishti targets defence and intelligence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring, and infrastructure planning. Conventional Earth observation systems are limited by weather and daylight — SAR works through clouds and at night, while optical sensors provide colour and spectral detail. Combining both on one platform means customers get reliable data regardless of conditions.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=dD_n22iK-8w

"With the satellite now successfully in orbit, our immediate focus is on completing its commissioning. We are already witnessing strong global interest in the differentiated datasets enabled by our OptoSAR payload."

— Suyash Singh, Founder and CEO, GalaxEye

The launch drew recognition at the highest levels. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it "a major achievement in our space journey" and "a testament to our youth's passion for innovation and nation-building." SpaceX founder Elon Musk responded with a public congratulations on X. Union Science Minister Jitendra Singh also highlighted the milestone as evidence of India's growing private space capabilities, the Hindu BusinessLine reported.

The Diaspora Connection

For Indian professionals in the global aerospace and defence supply chain — particularly in the US, where the satellite launched — Drishti signals that Indian startups are moving from component suppliers to system-level competitors. The company's Data-as-a-Service model could attract diaspora entrepreneurs and investors looking at dual-use space technology, a sector where cross-border expertise and capital flows between India and the West are accelerating.

What's Next

GalaxEye's immediate priority is completing Drishti's commissioning phase to begin delivering commercial data products. The company plans to scale to a constellation of 8 to 12 satellites by 2030, aiming for sub-daily revisit capability and broader global coverage. That expansion will require significant additional capital and manufacturing capacity — both areas where India's growing space ecosystem and its diaspora investor networks will be tested.
